coherence.reasons: Both run diagnosis, sized levers, sequencing, then risks, and in both the titles carry the argument. Y's five sub-questions map cleanly to its sections. Its weakness is that the governing thought promises 3.2%, while its own backup shows 2.7% once the known 2027 wage rise is counted; the headline only holds if the stretch levers are pulled. X's governing thought (about 2.9–3.1%) matches its base and stretch cases, with the wage step already inside the bridge, and its options table, one-time cost budget and gates all reconcile to the same $40.7M. X's slide 3 framing of its own 'initial hypothesis' is a little confusing, but it does not break the hierarchy.

judgment.reasons: X weighs five explicit options (management draft, recommended, without the three stores, plus exiting home delivery, grow e-commerce) with operating income, margin, one-time cost and constraint fit for each. It keeps labor action small (3% gross trim in the high-labor half, 1% reinvested in low-labor stores) with a reversal trigger, nets a 1% volume loss against the promotion cut, and reserves $2M for everyday prices near ValuMart. It also has stage gates and a sized contingency. Y's plan is defensible and handles the ValuMart trade-off well by keeping promotions within three miles. But its net 4% cut concentrated in Q3–Q4 stores implies roughly an 8% or deeper cut in those stores, and it simply assumes shrink is unchanged there. It also assumes no volume loss from cutting promotions, leaves the wage rise out of the base case, and rules exiting home delivery out of scope rather than weighing it. Y gives no one-time cost budget beyond the $7.5M lease exit.

evidence.reasons: Both get the critical numbers right: the bridge (gross margin −$15.3M, e-commerce −$12.6M, labor −$4.5M), the −$10.4M e-commerce drag, about −$12.34 per delivered order, the fee-test rollout at $2.5–2.8M, and $6.6M from store exits. Y adds a useful netting of $1.3M of double-counting in store exits and rebuilds the fulfillment line for all three years. X is more careful on inference: it flags the shrink-by-quartile pattern as a correlation, labels its $10M shrink analogy as illustrative, quantifies why the category team's comp claim does not prove profit, and marks every one-time cost except the lease exit as an assumption. It also spots that FY2026 closes as the board meets. Y makes weaker inferences: 'deeper promotions have not held off ValuMart' has no counterfactual, the promotion reset assumes zero volume loss, and the covenant test treats FY2026 as a plan year still ahead (though it flags this). Y's payback of 3.4 years omits closure costs.

revision.reasons: Both correctly revise management's wage hypothesis using a quantified bridge and the wage-versus-hours decomposition, and both replace the 8% blanket cut with a targeted one. X goes further: it values the management plan as a full option (0.9–1.7%, misses target), addresses the e-commerce freeze explicitly (keep growth frozen but reprice), and tests its own counter-hypothesis that commercial fixes alone suffice, finding they reach only about 2.1%. That is why it adds labor rebalancing and store exits. Y's revision is sound but retains a larger labor cut (half of management's) on a thinner shrink argument and does not address the freeze directly.

overall.reasons: Both documents reach a defensible, sized plan of the kind the answer key prefers and avoid the main traps. X serves the CEO better because its headline is honest: 2.9% base after the known wage step, 3.1% with stretch, and a 2.0–3.8% range. It budgets the $25M cap line by line, tells the board what to decide, sets gates and contingencies, and weighs more alternatives, including exiting home delivery. Y is clear and well structured, but its 3.2% headline excludes the 2027 wage rise, its promotion sizing assumes no volume loss, its labor cut carries under-examined shrink risk, and its covenant logic rests on a year that has already ended.
